notes.meaning: The Lord sent a message to the prophet Jehu son of Hanani to confront King Baasha. Jehu was a young prophet whose father Hanani was also a prophet who had boldly spoken to the king of Judah. Jehu obeyed God and delivered the warning even though rebuking an earthly king was very dangerous.

God reminded Baasha that He had raised him up from humble beginnings and made him ruler over Israel. Yet Baasha chose the same evil path as Jeroboam, leading God's people into idol worship and provoking His anger. Even though Baasha gained the throne through his own violent plot, God remained sovereign over his rise.

The Lord announced that Baasha's royal family would be completely wiped out. His dynasty would suffer the exact same ruin that destroyed the family of Jeroboam. Because Baasha copied Jeroboam's sins, his household would receive Jeroboam's punishment.

Anyone from Baasha's household who died inside a city would be eaten by wild dogs. Anyone who died out in the countryside would be eaten by vultures and birds. Leaving bodies unburied for scavengers was seen as a terrible disgrace in the ancient world.

The other events of Baasha's reign, including his power and accomplishments, were recorded in the official historical annals of Israel's kings. These state records documented his political success and military efforts. Earthly power cannot protect a king from God's righteous judgment.

Baasha died a natural death and was buried with honor in the capital city of Tirzah. His son Elah then took the throne in his place. Although Baasha personally escaped a violent death, the promised judgment soon fell upon his son.

The writer explains again why God sent Jehu against Baasha and his family. Baasha had provoked God by continuing Jeroboam's idol worship and by murdering King Nadab. Even though God permitted Jeroboam's line to fall, Baasha's violent coup was still a wicked murder in God's eyes.

Elah became king of Israel during King Asa's twenty-sixth year over Judah, and he ruled in Tirzah for two years. His time on the throne was actually less than two full years. This very brief reign showed that God's favor was not upon Baasha's family.

Elah stayed behind in the capital and got drunk at the home of Arza, his palace manager. Meanwhile, an army chariot commander named Zimri conspired to overthrow him. Elah acted foolishly by drinking while his troops were away risking their lives in battle.

Zimri walked in and struck down Elah during Asa's twenty-seventh year of reigning in Judah. Zimri murdered his master while he was in a drunken state and claimed the throne. This swift betrayal quickly cut short Elah's brief rule.

As soon as Zimri was crowned king, he slaughtered every male member of Baasha's family. He went even further by killing all their male relatives and friends so no one could avenge Elah's death. Zimri acted with total ruthlessness to secure his new power.

Zimri wiped out Baasha's entire household, exactly as the Lord had announced through the prophet Jehu. While Zimri acted purely for his own selfish gain, God used his violence to fulfill His prophetic word. God's warnings to sinful leaders always come true.

This total ruin fell upon the royal house because of the sins of Baasha and his son Elah. They had dragged the people of Israel into sin and angered the Lord with their empty golden calf idols. Serving worthless idols instead of the living God destroyed their whole family line.

The remaining events of Elah's life and all that he accomplished were documented in the official history of the kings of Israel. The biblical writer points readers to those royal archives for additional details. The Bible records only what matters for showing God's spiritual assessment of a ruler.

Zimri managed to rule in Tirzah for only seven days. During that week, Israel's army was camped near the Philistine town of Gibbethon, trying to capture it. Zimri carried out his bloody coup in the capital while the nation's military was away fighting.

News reached the army camp that Zimri had conspired against the king and murdered him. Right there in the camp, the soldiers rejected Zimri and proclaimed their army general Omri as king over Israel. The troops refused to let a traitor seize the throne.

Omri and the Israelite army immediately raised the siege at Gibbethon and marched up into the hills to Tirzah. They surrounded the capital city to remove Zimri from power. Omri moved swiftly to strike before the usurper could consolidate his rule.

When Zimri saw that Tirzah was captured, he retreated into the strongest citadel of the royal palace. He set the building on fire over himself and perished in the flames. He chose suicide rather than falling into the hands of his victorious rival.

Zimri died under God's judgment because of his wicked choices and his support of Jeroboam's idolatry. Even in his seven days on the throne, he gave clear signs that he would keep worshipping the golden calves. His sudden end was a fitting punishment for his treason and rebellion against God.

The rest of Zimri's deeds and the full story of his treason were kept in the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The biblical record shares little about him because his entire reign consisted only of a short, violent revolt. His rebellion left behind nothing of lasting honor.

After Zimri perished, the people of Israel split into two rival factions. Half of the people wanted Tibni son of Ginath to be king, while the other half supported Omri. This sharp division plunged the nation into several years of civil war.

Omri's forces proved stronger in battle than the followers of Tibni. Tibni died during the struggle, leaving Omri in complete control of the kingdom. With his rival gone, Omri was finally able to establish his own royal dynasty.

Omri began his sole reign in the thirty-first year of King Asa of Judah and ruled twelve years in all. This total includes the four years of civil war against Tibni, followed by eight years of peaceful rule. He ruled from the capital of Tirzah for the first six years before relocating.

Omri bought a prominent hill from a man named Shemer for two talents of silver and built a new capital city called Samaria. The hill stood in a central location, was easy to defend, and overlooked major travel routes. Samaria remained the capital city of northern Israel for the rest of the kingdom's history.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists and historians suggest Samaria began mostly as an administrative and royal compound rather than a large population center.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic historians note that Omri established Samaria in his sixth year and worked to turn former hostility toward Judah into peaceful relations.

notes.meaning: Omri did evil in the eyes of the Lord and acted worse than any king before him. He not only embraced Jeroboam's calf worship but even passed official statutes compelling the people to practice idolatry. His decrees locked the nation into deeper spiritual rebellion.

Omri walked in all the corrupt ways of Jeroboam and led the people of Israel into the same sin. They provoked the Lord to anger with their worthless, lifeless idols. Following man-made gods dragged the entire kingdom away from the living God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Assyrian inscriptions continued to refer to Israel as the 'house of Omri' long after his dynasty ended, showing that neighboring nations viewed him as a major political power.

notes.meaning: The other acts of Omri and the great military power he showed were recorded in the annals of Israel's kings. Even though the Bible describes his reign briefly, outside nations respected his military strength. God evaluates rulers by their spiritual loyalty rather than their political fame.

Omri died a natural death and was buried in his newly founded capital of Samaria. His son Ahab then became king in his place. Omri left behind a strong political kingdom, but his family would soon lead Israel into unprecedented spiritual wickedness.

Ahab became king of Israel during the thirty-eighth year of Asa's reign over Judah, and he ruled in Samaria for twenty-two years. His reign lasted as long as Jeroboam's original rule over the northern tribes. During Ahab's era, the nation plunged into its deepest spiritual crisis.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic scholars point out differences between biblical dates for Ahab and Assyrian records, suggesting the chronological figures in verse 29 may have undergone early copyist adjustments.

notes.meaning: Ahab committed more evil in the sight of the Lord than every king who ruled before him. Previous kings had worshipped the Lord through forbidden golden calves, but Ahab went much further by welcoming pagan gods into Israel. His reign marked a disastrous turning point away from the Lord.

Ahab treated Jeroboam's sins as a trivial thing and married Jezebel, the daughter of King Ethbaal of the Sidonians. Under her influence, Ahab began openly worshipping and serving the Canaanite god Baal. This marriage allied Israel with aggressive foreign idolatry and unleashed terrible religious persecution.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars observe that Ahab gave his children names honoring the Lord, suggesting he may have sought a political compromise between religions rather than completely abandoning the God of Israel.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic sources note that Jezebel's father was a priest of Astarte and that the marriage was designed as an alliance against Syria, allowing Jezebel to aggressively promote Phoenician worship in Israel.

notes.meaning: Ahab built a temple for Baal in the capital city of Samaria and set up a sacrificial altar inside it. By giving Baal a permanent house in the royal city, he made pagan worship an official state religion. He directly rebelled against God by putting a false god at the center of the nation.

Ahab made an Asherah pole, which was a cult object used to worship a Canaanite goddess associated with Baal. He did more to provoke the Lord God of Israel to anger than all the kings who came before him. His public devotion to foreign gods dragged the entire nation into shameless idolatry.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historians suggest Ahab established worship sites for Baal and Asherah alongside devotion to the Lord as a state policy to unite the Canaanite and Israelite factions of his kingdom.

notes.meaning: During Ahab's reign, a man named Hiel from Bethel rebuilt the fortified city of Jericho. Hiel lost his oldest son Abiram when laying its foundation and his youngest son Segub when hanging its gates. This tragedy fulfilled the solemn curse that Joshua had spoken against Jericho centuries earlier.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Hiel may have offered his sons as pagan foundation sacrifices during the construction, rather than having them die from disease or accidents.
